description.p: TREATMENT OF WILT DISEASES
Field of the Invention
This invention relates to the prevention or treatment of vascular wilt diseases of plants.
Background of the Invention

Vascular wilt diseases affect a wide variety of plant species, including valuable crop plants and ornamental plants, bushes and trees. These diseases are caused by a variety of plant pathogens, each of which attacks a particular range of host plants. The pathogen multiplies in and spreads through the vascular system of the attacked plant, interfering with water transport in the plant and producing progressive wilting of leaves and shoots, eventually leading to death of the plant if unchecked. Fire Blight Disease is one example of an aggressive and economically important vascular wilt disease, caused by the bacterium Erwinia amylovora. This organism attacks members of the family Rosaceae, which is a huge family including many members of commercial importance such as members of the genera Malus (apples), Pyrus (pears), Prunus (apricots, cherries, plums) and Rosa (roses). The host range of E. amylovora has been estimated to include nearly forty genera and over one hundred and thirty species.

The disease causes blackening of the succulent tissue of newly formed shoots, blight of the blossoms and fruitlets and the formation of cankers, giving the appearance of a plant scorched by fire and hence the name of the disease (Barny, (1990), Mol. Micro., A, 111).

Rain splash, insects, birds and humans are some of the common vectors for transmission of the pathogen. The most common vectors, however, are pollinators such as bees, flies and other insects. Infection begins on stigmas and nectarthodes, fresh wounds on any plant parts and stomata and lenticels on succulent twigs. From there, the bacteria move rapidly into the vascular system of the host plant, resulting in systemic infection and the symptoms associated with the disease (Bellemann and
Geider, J. General Microbiology 138, (1992), pp. 931-840; Momol et al., Plant Disease 82, (1998), pp. 646-650; and Bogs et al., Phytopathology 88, (1998), pp. 416-421).

Fire Blight Disease (FBD) first appeared in the north eastern parts of North America approximately 200 years ago. It has since spread to New Zealand in 1916, England in 1957, and is prevalent in the Middle East and the Mediterranean.

Numerous approaches have been employed to prevent or treat FBD or to limit its spread. The use of pesticides to control the insect vectors of the disease is not a viable option since many of the FBD vectors are desirable pollinating insects required for fruit production. One approach to controlling FBD has been to control the bacteria with antibiotic treatment. Unfortunately, £. amylovora is becoming progressively more resistant to antibiotic treatment with streptomycin (Lindow et al., Phytopathology 86, (1996), pp. 841-848; Loper et al., Plant Disease 75, (1991), pp. 287-290; and Moller et al., Plant Disease 65, (1981), pp. 563-568). Additionally, the indiscriminate use of antibiotics is undesirable from a human health standpoint and many countries actually prohibit the use of medically important antibiotics for plant disease control. There remains, therefore, a need for improved treatment to prevent or control outbreaks of FBD.

It has been shown that a glycoprotein produced by the fungus Ophiostoma ulmi, which causes Dutch Elm Disease (DED) in elm trees, can be used to protect elm trees against attack by the fungus, by stimulating a defence reaction against the fungus in treated elm trees (PCT/CA98/00284). It was not suspected, however, that this glycoprotein would be useful to combat diseases other than DED.
Summary of the Invention

As used herein, except where clearly indicated otherwise by the context, "vascular wilt disease" means a vascular wilt disease other than Dutch Elm Disease (DED). It has been shown previously that the DED-producing fungus

Ophiostoma ulmi produces "elicitor" compounds which can elicit a defence reaction in elm trees, whereby the elm trees produce compounds inhibitory to. the fungus and are thus enabled to resist infection.

The inventor has isolated and characterised one such elicitor compound produced by 0. ulmi which is a glycoprotein. A DNA molecule encoding the protein chain of this glycoprotein elicitor has been cloned and sequenced (Sequence ID NO:1) and its amino acid sequence has been determined (Sequence ID NO:3).

The inventor has shown that, surprisingly, this glycoprotein elicitor obtainable from a DED-causing fungus confers resistance against vascular wilt diseases other than DED on plants susceptible to vascular wilt diseases other than DED.

The invention provides a method for inducing resistance to a vascular wilt disease in a susceptible plant by administering to the plant a glycoprotein elicitor obtainable from a DED-causing fungus in an amount effective to produce resistance.
Detailed Description of the Invention

In accordance with one embodiment, the invention provides a method for inducing resistance to a vascular wilt disease in a susceptible plant by administering to the plant a glycoprotein elicitor obtainable from a DED- causing fungus in an amount effective to produce resistance.

Plants which are susceptible to vascular wilt diseases and may benefit from the treatment of the invention include trees, shrubs, woody perennials and non-woody plants.
For example, wilt diseases can be caused by Verticillium spp which attack maples and elms, as well as non-woody plants such as alfalfa and potatoes; Ceratocystis fagacearum (Oak Wilt) which attacks oaks; and Fusarium spp. which attack a variety of plants including tomatoes, coffee plants and herbs.

In accordance with a preferred embodiment, the invention provides a method for inducing resistance to FBD in a susceptible plant by administering, to the plant a glycoprotein elicitor obtainable from a DED-causing fungus. FBD is caused by E. amylovora which attacks members of the Rosaceae family which includes the following genera and species:

Amelanchier (serviceberry), Exchorda (pearlbush), Potentilla (cinquefoil), Aroma (chokeberry), Fragaria (strawberry), Prinsepia, Aruncus (goatsbeard), Ceum (avnes), Prunus (apricot, cherry, plum), Chaenomeles (flowering quince), Heteromeles (toyon), Pyracantha (firethorn), Cotoneaster (cottoneaster), Holodiscus (creambush), Pyrus (pear), Cowania (cliff rose), Kageneckia, Raphiolepes (Indian hawthorn), Crataegomespilus, Kerria (Japanese rose), Rhodotypos Getbead), Crataegus (hawthorn), Malus (apple, crabapple), Rosa (rose) Cydonia (quince), Mespilus (medlar), rubus (brambles), Dichotomanthes, Osteomeles, Sorbaria (false spirea), Docynia, Peraphyllum, Sorbus (mountain ash), Dryas (mountain avens), Photinia
(photinia), Spiraea (spiraea), Eriobotrya (loquat), Physocarpus (ninebark) and Stranvaesia.
Treatment with the glycoprotein elicitors described herein has been shown to protect FBD-susceptible plants such as apples and pears against subsequent challenge with inoculations of E. amylovora.

This is a novel approach to the control of FBD, since the glycoprotein elicitor is a non-toxic, environmentally friendly substance which apparently induces the FBD-susceptible plant's defence mechanisms and thereby confers resistance against the FBD pathogen. Glycoprotein elicitors for use in the method of the invention are obtainable from the DED-causing fungus, O.ulmi.
The elicitor may be isolated from whole cells, cell walls, or the cell interior of 0. ulmi or from culture filtrates. Non-aggressive strains of 0. ulmi are preferred and strain 0. ulmi Q412 is especially preferred.

A DNA sequence has been cloned which encodes a glycoprotein elicitor produced by O. ulmi. The complete coding region, including one intron, and portions of the 5' and 3' untranslated sequences are shown in Sequence ID NO:1 ; the open reading frame commences at nucleotide 197 of that sequence and nucleotides 927 to 988 are the intron. Sequence ID NO:2 shows the nucleotides of the open reading frame without the intron and the corresponding amino acid sequence. The elicitor gene encodes a protein of 409 amino acids (Sequence ID NO:3).

Based on homology comparisons with published gene sequences, the O. ulmi elicitor shows the greatest homology to asparatic proteinases from fungi such as Glomerella cingulata (65.6% homology), Podospora anserian (62.6% homology), Rhizopus chinensis (51.8% homology) and Cryphonectria (Endothia) parasitica (62.6% homology).

In general, asparatic proteinases are a group of proteinases that possess two catalytic asparatyl residues and have a variety of important biological functions such as programmed cell death (apoptosis) . Although asparatic proteinases are widely dispersed in the animal and plant kingdom, and have been isolated from bacteria and the HIV virus, only relatively few are glycoproteins. Furthermore, although some pathogen asparatic proteinases have been linked to virulence factors of their producers, none have been shown to induce resistance in their hosts. It is believed that DED-causing fungi such as 0. ulmi produce further elicitors having a high degree of homology to the amino acid sequence of Sequence ID NO:3.

The protein component of the glycoprotein elicitor described herein may also act as an elicitor conferring resistance to vascular wilt diseases, as described herein, in the absence of attached sugars.
This further embodiment, using the protein without sugars, or effective fragments thereof, to confer disease resistance, is also included within the scope of this invention.
In accordance with one embodiment, the invention provides isolated nucleic acids corresponding to or related to the nucleic acid sequences disclosed herein which encode an elicitor.

One of ordinary skill in the art is now enabled to identify and isolate genes which are homologues of the gene disclosed herein, either additional genes of 0. ulmi or homologues from other microorganisms, using standard hybridisation screening or PCR techniques.
In one embodiment, the invention provides nucleic acids comprising the nucleotide sequences designated Sequence ID NO:1 and 2.

Also provided are portions of the gene disclosed herein useful as probes in PCR primers or for encoding fragments of the elicitor. The invention provides isolated nucleic acid sequences comprising sequences corresponding to at least 10, preferably at least 15 and more preferably at least 20 consecutive nucleotides of the nucleic acids disclosed herein.
The invention further includes any of the described nucleotide sequences included in a vector.
In accordance with a further embodiment, the invention provides substantially pure elicitor proteins, fragments of these proteins and fusion proteins including these proteins or fragments.
In a further embodiment, the invention provides a substantially pure protein comprising the amino acid sequence of Sequence ID NO:3.

The invention further provides substantially pure polypeptides which comprise fragments of the amino acid sequence disclosed herein. These may comprise amino acid sequences corresponding to at least 10, preferably at least 20 and more preferably 50 to 100 consecutive amino acids of Sequence ID NO:3.
The invention includes proteins having an amino acid sequence of greater than 70%, preferably greater than 80% and more preferably greater than 90% overall identity to the amino acid sequence of Sequence ID NO:3.

The present invention also includes within its scope all elicitors obtainable from DED-causing fungi, and effective fragments and analogues thereof, which cause a defence reaction in wilt disease susceptible plants, the defence reaction comprising the accumulation of wilt disease-inhibitory compounds in the plants.
"Analogue" includes any functional equivalent of an elicitor protein, including proteins having one or more conservative amino acid substitutions and proteins incorporating unnatural amino acids.

The proteins of the invention may be prepared by recombinant expression of the nucleic acid sequences disclosed herein in a suitable host, as will be understood by those of ordinary skill in the art. For protein expression, eukaryotic or prokaryotic expression systems may be generated in which an elicitor gene sequence is introduced into a plasmid or other vector which is then introduced into living cells. Constructs in which the elicitor DNA sequence containing the entire open reading frame is inserted in the correct orientation into an expression plasmid may be used for protein expression. Alternatively, portions of the sequence may be inserted. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic expression systems allow various important functional domains of the protein to be recovered as fusion proteins and used for binding, structural and functional studies and also for the generation of appropriate antibodies. Typical expression vectors contain promoters that direct the synthesis of large amounts of mRNA corresponding to the gene. They may also include sequences allowing for their autonomous replication within the host organism, sequences that encode genetic traits that allow cells containing the vectors to be selected, and sequences that increase the efficiency with which the mRNA is translated. Stable long-term vectors may be maintained as freely replicating entities by using regulatory elements of viruses. Cell lines may
also be produced which have integrated the vector into the genomic DNA and in this manner the gene product is produced on a continuous basis.

Expression of foreign sequences in bacteria such as E. coli require the insertion of the sequence into an expression vector, usually a plasmid which contains several elements such as sequences encoding a selectable marker that assures maintenance of the vector in the cell, a controllable transcriptional promoter which upon induction can produce large amounts of mRNA from the cloned gene, translational control sequences and a polylinker to simplify insertion of the gene in the correct orientation within the vector. A relatively simple E. coli expression system utilizes the lac promoter and a neighboring lacZ gene which is cut out of the expression vector with restriction enzymes and replaced by the elicitor gene sequence. In vitro expression of proteins encoded by cloned DNA is also possible using the T7 late-promoter expression system. Plasmid vectors containing late promoters and the corresponding RNA polymerases from related bacteriophages such as T3, T5 and SP6 may also be used for in vitro production of proteins from cloned DNA. E. coli can also be used for expression by infection with M13 Phage mGPI-2. E. coli vectors can also be used with phage Lambda regulatory sequences, by fusion protein vectors, by maltose-binding protein fusions, and by glutathione-S-transferase fusion proteins.

Eukaryotic expression systems permit appropriate post-translational modifications to expressed proteins. This allows for studies of the elicitor genes and gene products including determination of proper expression and post-translational modifications for biological activity, identifying regulatory elements in the 5' region of the gene and their role in regulation of protein expression. It also permits the production of large amounts of normal proteins for isolation and purification.

The elicitor DNA sequences can be altered using procedures such as restriction enzyme digestion, DNA polymerase fill-in, exonuclease deletion, terminal deoxynucleotide transferase extension, ligation of synthetic or cloned
DNA sequences and site-directed in vitro mutagenesis, including site-directed sequence alteration using specific oligonucleotides together with PCR.

Once the appropriate expression vector containing the selected gene is constructed, it is introduced into an appropriate host cell by transformation techniques including calcium phosphate transfection, DEAE-dextran transfection, electroporation, microinjection, protoplast fusion and liposome- mediated transfection.

The host cell which may be transfected with a vector of this invention may be selected from the group consisting of E. Coli, Pseudomonas, Bacillus subtilis, or other bacilli, other bacteria, yeast, fungi, insect (using baculoviral vectors for expression), mouse or other animal or human tissue cells.
Mammalian cells can also be used to express the elicitor proteins using a vaccinia virus expression system.

Methods for producing appropriate vectors, for transforming cells with those vectors and for identifying transformants are described in the scientific literature, for example in Sambrook et al. (1989), Molecular Cloning: A
Laboratory Manual, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press, Cold Spring
Harbor, N.Y. or latest edition thereof.

The elicitors of the invention may also be prepared by culturing 0. ulmi. In accordance with a preferred embodiment, a culture of 0. ulmi is initiated from a mycelial plug and incubated for about 10 days on a culture medium, for example Wilson's medium. After incubation, the spores and mycelium are removed by centrifugation and the polysaccharides are removed by precipitation and filtering of the medium. The medium is then passed through a PM10 ultrafiiter to produce a concentrated protein fraction containing at least one elicitor, which is then lyophilized.
It is to be appreciated that elicitors according to the invention may be produced on a large scale from cultures of DED-causing fungi, preferably

0. ulmi, incubated in a fermenter. It is to be further appreciated that elicitors according to the present invention do not need to be purified before being used. Rather, the elicitors
may be used in crude or partially purified form.

Elicitors according to the invention are non-toxic, generally heat stable, and may be stored in powder form indefinitely without adverse consequences. The stability of the elicitors allows them to be administered to trees in a variety of forms. Preferably, elicitors are administered in solid form or liquid form. Preferred solid forms include tablets or capsules, and preferred liquid forms include injectable compositions.

The elicitors according to the present invention are administered to plants in an amount sufficient to produce a defence reaction in the plant, in which sufficient anti-bacterial activity is elicited to provide the tree with resistance to FBD.

The preferred dose of elicitor depends on a variety of factors, including the time of the year, size and vigour of the tree. However, the inventor has observed that small doses of elicitor may be as effective as larger doses to induce resistance in trees.

For example, the inventor has found that for trees having trunk diameters (at breast height) ranging from about 20cm to greater than 100cm, doses of at least about 5mg of elicitor are preferred. More preferably, the amount of elicitor administered is from about 5 mg to about 150 mg, and most preferably from about 10 mg to about 80 mg. Ranges of the elicitor of about 0.1 mg to about 150 mg can be effective under some circumstances.

When administered in solid form, elicitors are preferably incorporated into a capsule which can be dissolved by the tree. Other ingredients, such as fillers and carriers, may also be added to the capsule as required. The capsule is preferably administered by drilling a small hole into the tree, preferably on its trunk or stem, and then inserting the capsule into the hole so that it becomes received inside the outer sapwood and bark of the tree. Suitable fillers or carriers include, for example, lactose or dextrose or mixtures thereof, and PVP may be used as binder. Tablets or capsules may be formed by conventional methods such as those employed to prepare pharmaceutical tablets and capsules.
The elicitors can also be applied as a paste to plant wounds, including wounds caused by tree pruning. Pastes may be formulated by conventional methods, employing for example gelatin or common gums and binding agents. When administered in liquid form, elicitors may be injected into plant stems, preferably in the case of trees through a small pre-drilled hole in the tree and preferably into the outer vascular system of the tree.
Preferably, the injectable composition comprises an aqueous solution of elicitors. The composition may comprise additional ingredients, such as carriers and cosolvents, as required.
Liquid compositions of elicitors may also be applied to plants as a foliar spray or as a spray used during the flowering period, since the elicitors are harmless to pollinating insects.

Liquid compositions of elicitors preferably comprise an aqueous solution containing the elicitor at concentrations ranging from about 0.1 to about 50 mg/mL. Other preferred ranges include preferably from about 0.5 to about 2 mg/mL and from 10 to about 50 mg/mL.

In accordance with a further embodiment, plants are protected against vascular wilt diseases by administration of elicitors so that they may be taken up by the plant roots, for example by application of a liquid composition containing the elicitors to the soil or other growing medium, for example a drench, a root injection, drip irrigation or a granular soil application. In accordance with a further embodiment, the elicitors are used as a seed treatment by applying a liquid or powder composition of elicitor to the seeds.

In accordance with a preferred embodiment, the elicitors are administered to susceptible perennials and trees annually, in order to provide adequate protection. Annual treatment is preferred so that the defence reaction triggered by the elicitor may occur in each newly formed annual tissue. Although at least partially dependent on climate, elicitors may be administered to plants at any time of year.
The elicitors of the invention may be used to treat plants already infected with a vascular wilt disease, for example FBD, or may be used preventatively to induce resistance in healthy plants. When used to treat infected plants, the elicitors induce resistance to the disease in parts of the plant which have not been infected, thereby preventing spread of disease to healthy parts of the plant. Preferably, dead or infected branches are cut off to further prevent spread of the disease.
EXAMPLES
Example 1
(a) Preparation of Elicitor

Elicitor was isolated from a 10 day old culture of Q412, a non- aggressive isolate of 0. ulmi. The culture was initiated from a mycelium plug maintained in 10% glycerol at -70°C. The culture media were prepared in 4L quantities in 15L Nalgene fermenter flasks and autoclaved at 121°C for 30 minutes. The fermenter flasks were inoculated with 25mL of a turbid spore suspension from a 3 day old culture. The flasks were incubated at 25°C with shaking at 125 rpm for 10 days. The spores were removed by centrifugation and the polysaccharides precipitated with an equal volume of ethanol. The precipitated culture broth was filtered through a Whatman #42 filter and the ethanol removed on a Buchi rotovapor under reduced pressure. The water component was subsequently filtered through a 0.22μm filter. The protein component was concentrated on a PM10 filter and lyophilized. The composition of the lyophilized product was analyzed by gel electrophoresis to verify the presence of the elicitor.

Injectable elicitor compositions were prepared by dissolving the lyophilized elicitor obtained as described above in distilled water.
(b) Treatment of Seedlings

35 Golden Delicious apple seedlings were grown in a greenhouse to a height of about 60 cm in single pots. 20 seedlings were randomly chosen and wounded as the control group, while 15 seedlings were treated with 20μl elicitor (20 mg/ml) by injection into the leaves at the apex of the plant.

One week after treatment, 10 seedlings from the control group (now designated Group 2) and 10 seedlings from the elicitor-treated group (Group 3) were challenged with the virulent £. amylovora strain E.a. 6-4 at a concentration of 108 CFU/ml by injection into the apex of the seedling. The remaining 5 seedlings from the elicitor-treated group (Group 4) were challenged 14 days later.
Group 1 consisted of the remaining 10 seedlings from the control group not infected with the pathogen. The results are shown in Table 1.

Example 6: Sequencing of Elicitor
(a) Isolates and Culture Conditions

An isolate of 0. ulmi was maintained on malt agar slants at -20°C for long-term storage. To prepare mycelium for DNA extractions, the isolate was sub-cultured for 7 days on modified Salemink medium containing 2% bacto-agar to form colonies. Mycelial disks, 5 x 5 mm in diameter, were then excised from the periphery of the colony and transferred into 125 mL Erlenmeyer flasks containing 50 mL of liquid modified Salesmink medium and incubated on a rotary shaker (150 rpm) at 25°C for 6 days to obtain budding yeast-phase cells. Budding yeast-phase cells were harvested by centrifugation at 1 ,110 x g for 20 mm. and lyophilized in a Labconco freeze dryer for 2 days.
(b) DNA Extraction, PCR Amplification and Cloning

Genomic DNA was extracted from lyophilized budding phase cells using DNeasy Plant Mini Kit (QIAGEN Inc., CA 91355) as described by the
supplier. Specific oligonucleotide primers derived from amino acid sequences were designed and used for PCR amplification.

Each PCR reaction contained 50 pmol of each primer, 50-100 ng of genomic DNA, 10 mM Tris-HCI, 1.5 mM MgCI2, 0.01% gelatin, 0.1% Triton X- I00, 1 unit of Taq DNA polymerase, 50 mM KCI and 200 μm each of dATP, dCTP, dGTP and dTTP in a final volume of 50μl. Amplification was performed under mineral oil in a thermal cycler (BIO/CAN) with the following cycle program: (1) 95°C for 3 min, (2) 35 times of (a) 95°C for 1 min, (b) 50°C for 50 s, (c) 72°C for 50 s, and (3) 72°C for 8 min. An aliquot of 3-5 μl of the PCR product from each reaction was cloned into the TA cloning vector, pCRII (Invitrogen, San Diego, CA 92121 ,
USA) following the manufacturer's instructions. Plasmid DNA containing PCR amplified product was verified by Eco Rl restriction digestion.
(c) DNA Seguencing

DNA sequencing was performed using double-stranded PCR- derived DNA which was sub-cloned into the plasmid vector pCRII. Sequence reactions were carried out with a T7 Sequencing kit (Pharmacia) using S[35] radiolabelled dATP and electrophoresized in a model S2 sequencing gel electrophoresis apparatus (Gibco BRL, Life Technologies) . The universal and reverse primers were used as sequencing primers to determine the DNA sequence.

A total of about 1200 bp nucleotides were constructed from various DNA sequences obtained above. Two primers (5'-GAC GGT/C CTC GTG/T GGT/C CTC GGT/C TTC and 5'-CCG TCG AAC/A/G ACC/A ACG AAG/C GC) were selected to amplify a DNA fragment of about 600 bp. This DNA fragment was used as a probe to isolate the elicitor gene from genomic library of O. ulmi. Genomic library was constructed using a Lambda FIX II genomic library kit (Stratagene). The genomic clone containing elicitor insert was then sequenced using various internal primers to obtain promoter as well as
terminator sequences. DNA sequence was performed using ABI PRISM automatic DNA sequencer.
The present invention is not limited to the features of the embodiments described herein, but includes all variations and modifications within the scope of the claims.
